note:
82-year-old male, urgent care visit for neuro c/o. Pt came w/ daughter (primary caregiver, lives w/ pt) who gives part of the hx.

CC: burning pain + numbness both feet x 6 mo, worse past 2 wk.

HPI:
Long-standing T2DM (~20 yrs), HTN, HLD, CKD 3a.
Burning + tingling soles bilat, stocking distribution to mid-calf, worse at night. Cold feet. Pt also c/o pins and needles in toes.
Still works rotating night shifts as security guard, irregular sched (3 nights, 2 days off, then 2 evening shifts). Pain worst when trying to sleep in daytime, sleeping only ~4 h/day. Misses meds when shifts change.
Daughter states pt tripped x2 past month on uneven pavement, no actual fall, no head strike.
Denies foot ulcers/open sores per pt. Daughter checked feet last wk, none seen.
Denies leg weakness, no back pain, no saddle numbness, no bowel/bladder incontinence, no fever.
No chest pain, no SOB.

Meds per pt: gabapentin 300 mg qHS only, metformin 500 mg BID, lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 81 mg daily. Also OTC ibuprofen 400 mg PRN for foot pain ~3x/wk and diphenhydramine 25 mg qHS for sleep.
Daughter brought bottles: gabapentin label reads 300 mg BID. Correction: gabapentin is 300 mg BID, not qHS only. Pt skips the AM dose on night-shift days.
NKDA.

VS: BP 148/82, HR 74, RR 16, SpO2 96% RA, Temp 98.2 F. POC glucose 164.
Exam: elderly M, NAD, A&O x3.
Feet: skin intact, dry, no ulcers/calluses/erythema. DP/PT pulses 1+ bilat, cap refill ~3 sec.
Monofilament absent over toes + forefoot bilat, present at heel. Vibration absent at great toes bilat. Pinprick decreased to mid-shin.
Ankle reflexes absent bilat, knee reflexes 1+. Strength 5/5, no foot drop.
Gait slow, wide-based, Romberg positive. No spinal tenderness.

Data: BMP Cr 1.3, eGFR 52, K 4.4, Na 139. CBC Hgb 12.9, WBC 7.2. POC A1c 7.9%.
XR both feet: no fracture, no Charcot changes, mild OA 1st MTP bilat.

Dx: painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy w/ sensory ataxia + gait instability -> fall risk.
T2DM, A1c ok for age, goal <8.
CKD 3a, renally dose meds.
Sleep deprivation from shift work + nocturnal pain.

Rx:
Gabapentin increase 300 mg BID -> 300 mg TID, 1st dose on waking, 2nd mid-shift, 3rd before sleep (timed to his wake/sleep, not the clock). Renal fxn ok for this dose. Counseled re dizziness/sedation.
STOP ibuprofen (CKD 3a, HTN, on aspirin). Acetaminophen 500 mg q6h PRN, max 3 g/day.
STOP diphenhydramine qHS (Beers, falls).
Cont metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin, aspirin, same doses.
Labs: B12 level (on metformin), TSH, urine ACR.
Referrals: outpt neuro for NCS/EMG, podiatry, PT for gait/balance.
Daughter to inspect feet daily. Pillbox + phone alarms set by wake time, not clock time.
Return precautions reviewed w/ pt + daughter: foot wound, redness, fever, new weakness, fall, urinary retention.
F/u PCP 1-2 wk.
summary: An 82-year-old male shift worker with long-standing T2DM presented to urgent care with 6 months of burning pain and numbness in both feet, with his daughter providing part of the history. Examination showed absent monofilament and vibration sensation, absent ankle reflexes, and a wide-based gait; A1c was 7.9% and eGFR 52. Assessment was painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy with gait instability, CKD 3a, and sleep deprivation. Gabapentin, first reported as bedtime only, was clarified from the bottle as 300 mg BID and increased to 300 mg TID, ibuprofen and diphenhydramine were stopped, and acetaminophen as needed was started. B12, TSH, and urine ACR were ordered, with neurology, podiatry, and PT referrals and PCP follow-up in 1-2 weeks.

His daughter, the primary caregiver, reports he tripped twice in the past month without falling or striking his head. Denies foot ulcers, open sores, leg weakness, back pain, saddle numbness, bowel/bladder incontinence, fever, chest pain, and SOB. History of T2DM (~20 years), HTN, HLD, CKD 3a. Medications: gabapentin first reported as 300 mg qHS only, corrected from the bottle label to 300 mg BID (skips the AM dose on night-shift days), metformin 500 mg BID, lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 81 mg daily, OTC ibuprofen 400 mg PRN about 3x/week, and diphenhydramine 25 mg qHS. NKDA.
soap.objective: BP 148/82, HR 74, RR 16, SpO2 96% RA, Temp 98.2 F, POC glucose 164. NAD, A&O x3. Feet: skin intact and dry without ulcers, calluses, or erythema; DP/PT pulses 1+ bilaterally, cap refill ~3 sec. Monofilament absent over toes and forefoot bilaterally, present at heel; vibration absent at great toes; pinprick decreased to mid-shin. Ankle reflexes absent bilaterally, knee reflexes 1+, strength 5/5, no foot drop. Gait slow and wide-based, Romberg positive, no spinal tenderness. BMP: Cr 1.3, eGFR 52, K 4.4, Na 139. CBC: Hgb 12.9, WBC 7.2. POC A1c 7.9%. XR both feet: no fracture, no Charcot changes, mild OA of the 1st MTP bilaterally.
soap.assessment: Painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy with sensory ataxia and gait instability (fall risk). T2DM with A1c acceptable for age (goal <8). CKD 3a requiring renal dosing of medications. Sleep deprivation from shift work and nocturnal pain.
plan: Increase gabapentin from 300 mg BID to 300 mg TID, first dose on waking, second mid-shift, third before sleep (timed to wake/sleep rather than the clock); counseled on dizziness and sedation
Stop ibuprofen (CKD 3a, HTN, on aspirin); acetaminophen 500 mg q6h PRN, max 3 g/day
Stop diphenhydramine qHS (Beers, falls)
Continue metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin, and aspirin at the same doses
Labs: B12 level (on metformin), TSH, urine ACR
Referrals: outpatient neurology for NCS/EMG, podiatry, PT for gait and balance
Daughter to inspect feet daily; pillbox and phone alarms set by wake time, not clock time
Return precautions reviewed with patient and daughter: foot wound, redness, fever, new weakness, fall, urinary retention
Follow up with PCP in 1-2 weeks

note:
The patient is a 67-year-old female seen in the geriatrics clinic for recurrent falls and a review of her medications. A professional medical interpreter was used for the entire visit, and the patient and I confirmed through the interpreter that she understood each question.

She reports three falls over the past four months, all at home at night while walking to the bathroom. She denies any loss of consciousness or head injury. She denies dizziness on standing, chest pain, palpitations, and new weakness. Her only chronic condition is hypertension, treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily. She has also taken zolpidem 10 mg at bedtime for sleep for several years. She brought a bag of bottles, and with the interpreter we removed expired and duplicate bottles from her home supply.

On examination, orthostatic blood pressure was 138/80 seated and 134/78 standing after three minutes, so there was no significant drop, and heart rate was 70. The Timed Up and Go took 16 seconds, which is slow. Her gait was slow with mild shuffling, Romberg was negative, and leg strength was 5/5 bilaterally.

My impression is recurrent falls, most likely related to sedation from zolpidem and poor night lighting, with hypertension that is well controlled. I will reduce zolpidem from 10 mg to 5 mg at bedtime for two weeks and then stop it, and I reviewed sleep habits. She will continue amlodipine. I am referring her to physical therapy for gait and balance training and arranging a home safety evaluation, including nightlights on the path to the bathroom. I ordered a vitamin D level, and she will return in four weeks.
summary: A 67-year-old female with hypertension was seen in the geriatrics clinic, with a professional interpreter, for three falls at night over four months and a medication review. She denied loss of consciousness, head injury, dizziness on standing, chest pain, palpitations, and new weakness. Orthostatic blood pressure showed no significant drop, but the Timed Up and Go was slow at 16 seconds with a slow, mildly shuffling gait. The impression was recurrent falls, likely related to zolpidem sedation and poor night lighting, with well-controlled hypertension. Zolpidem will be reduced to 5 mg at bedtime for two weeks and then stopped, amlodipine continued, and physical therapy, a home safety evaluation, and a vitamin D level arranged with follow-up in four weeks.

note:
Telehealth visit note, nephrology follow-up.
Visit modality: audio-only telephone visit. Identity confirmed with two identifiers and verbal consent for a telephone visit obtained. No video was available, so no visual exam was performed. The patient was at home.

Reason for visit: follow-up of chronic kidney disease stage 3b in a 43-year-old female, and review of recent labs.

Patient-reported history: She has had type 2 diabetes for 11 years and hypertension for 9 years, and her kidney function has been slowly declining. Over the past month she has felt more tired and notes mild ankle swelling by the end of the day. She also notes foamy urine, unchanged from before. She denies shortness of breath, chest pain, nausea, vomiting, itching, and gross hematuria. She denies decreased urine output.

Cost and adherence: She stopped taking empagliflozin 10 mg daily about 6 weeks ago because the copay at the pharmacy became too high after her insurance plan changed. She takes sodium bicarbonate 650 mg only once a day instead of BID to make the supply last, and she skips amlodipine on some days when money is tight.

Medication reconciliation: She first stated that she takes lisinopril 20 mg daily. After reading the label on her bottle during the call, she corrected this: the bottle says losartan 50 mg once daily, and she has never been prescribed lisinopril. Other medications: amlodipine 5 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg BID, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg as needed for knee pain about three times a week. No known drug allergies.

Home measurements: BP 148/90, 152/92, and 146/88 on three mornings this week with her home cuff, HR 78, weight 182 lb and stable, fingerstick glucose 142 this morning.

Data reviewed (drawn last week): Cr 1.9, eGFR 34, K 5.1, bicarbonate 20, Hgb 10.4, phos 4.8, PTH 112, UACR 640 mg/g, and A1c 7.6%. Her eGFR was 38 three months ago.

Impression: chronic kidney disease stage 3b, likely diabetic and hypertensive kidney disease, with eGFR down from 38 to 34, albuminuria, mild metabolic acidosis, mild hyperkalemia, and anemia of CKD. Blood pressure is above goal. Cost-related non-adherence is the main driver, and ibuprofen use is a further risk for kidney injury.

Discussed with the patient by phone:
Increase amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg daily. Continue losartan 50 mg once daily and do not increase it until potassium is rechecked.
Reduce metformin from 1000 mg BID to 500 mg BID because of the eGFR of 34.
Stop ibuprofen. For knee pain use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed, maximum 3 g per day.
Resume sodium bicarbonate 650 mg BID; the generic is low cost at her pharmacy.
Refer to the clinic pharmacist and social worker to apply for a patient assistance program for empagliflozin, to be restarted once it is affordable.
Repeat BMP in 1 week. Order ferritin and TSAT for the anemia. Repeat UACR in 3 months.
Dietitian referral for a low-potassium, low-sodium diet.
Teach-back was completed and she repeated the medication changes accurately. Telephone follow-up in 2 weeks and nephrology clinic in 3 months. She should go to the emergency department for chest pain, severe weakness, shortness of breath, or very little urine.
summary: A 43-year-old female with chronic kidney disease stage 3b, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension had a telephone nephrology follow-up and reported underusing medications because of cost, including stopping empagliflozin. Home blood pressures were about 148/90, and recent labs showed Cr 1.9, eGFR 34, K 5.1, Hgb 10.4, and UACR 640 mg/g. She first named lisinopril but corrected this to losartan 50 mg once daily after reading the bottle. Amlodipine was increased to 10 mg daily, metformin reduced to 500 mg BID, ibuprofen stopped, and sodium bicarbonate resumed, with pharmacy and social work help for empagliflozin, repeat BMP in 1 week, and follow-up in 2 weeks.

note:
Dictating a gynecology consult note on the ward. The patient is a 20-year-old female on hospital day 2 for dehydration from viral gastroenteritis, which is improving. She was also hospitalized three weeks ago for pyelonephritis and received IV antibiotics followed by ten days of oral antibiotics. Since finishing those she reports vulvar itching and thick white vaginal discharge. This is her third episode in the past year, correction, her fourth episode in the past year, and the earlier ones came back after over-the-counter cream. She denies fever, pelvic pain, abnormal bleeding, and foul odor. She has no chronic medical conditions and no known drug allergies.

On exam temperature is 98.4, blood pressure 112/70, heart rate 76. External genitalia show mild erythema of the vulva. There is thick white curd-like discharge adherent to the vaginal walls, the cervix looks normal, and there is no cervical motion tenderness or adnexal tenderness. Vaginal pH is 4.2, KOH prep is positive for pseudohyphae, whiff test is negative, and I see no clue cells or trichomonads. Urine pregnancy test is negative. A NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhea was sent.

Impression is recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, likely triggered by her recent antibiotic course. She will start fluconazole 150 mg every 72 hours for three doses, then 150 mg once weekly for six months, and I counseled her to avoid unnecessary antibiotics and to keep the area dry. I will call her with the NAAT results, and she will follow up in the gynecology clinic in two weeks. That completes the dictation.

She denied fever, pelvic pain, abnormal bleeding, and foul odor. Exam showed vulvar erythema and curd-like discharge, vaginal pH was 4.2, KOH prep showed pseudohyphae, and the urine pregnancy test was negative. The impression was recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, likely triggered by recent antibiotics. Fluconazole 150 mg every 72 hours for three doses, then weekly for six months, was prescribed, with NAAT results to be called and gynecology follow-up in two weeks.

note:
Telehealth visit note, cardiology follow-up.
Visit modality: audio-only telephone visit with the patient at home. Identity verified and verbal consent for a telephone visit obtained. No video, so no physical exam was possible.

Reason for visit: 3-week follow-up after an NSTEMI treated with a drug-eluting stent to the proximal LAD in a 71-year-old female with hypertension and hyperlipidemia.

Interval history (patient-reported): She was discharged 3 weeks ago and feels steadily better. She walks 15 minutes twice daily without symptoms. She reports mild fatigue in the afternoons. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, lightheadedness, and leg swelling. She denies black stools, blood in her urine, nosebleeds, and unusual bruising while on dual antiplatelet therapy. She reports taking all medications as prescribed with no missed doses.

Home measurements: BP 138/84 (average of 5 readings this week), HR 62, weight 156 lb and stable.

Medications: aspirin 81 mg daily, ticagrelor 90 mg BID, atorvastatin 80 mg daily, and metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily.

Data reviewed: Inpatient echo showed LVEF 50% with mild anterior hypokinesis. Admission LDL was 118 mg/dL. Creatinine at discharge was 0.9.

Impression: NSTEMI s/p drug-eluting stent to the proximal LAD, 3 weeks out, clinically stable without angina. Hypertension above goal on home readings. Hyperlipidemia on a high-intensity statin, with LDL to be rechecked.

Orders and counseling: start lisinopril 5 mg daily for blood pressure and post-MI LV protection, with a BMP 1 to 2 weeks after starting. Continue aspirin 81 mg daily and ticagrelor 90 mg BID without interruption for 12 months. Continue atorvastatin 80 mg daily and metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. Fasting lipid panel in 6 weeks, and lipid therapy will be reassessed if LDL remains above 70. Refer to cardiac rehab. Reviewed warning signs and to call 911 for chest pain not relieved by rest. Clinic follow-up with ECG in 6 weeks.
summary: A 71-year-old female with hypertension and hyperlipidemia had a telephone cardiology follow-up 3 weeks after an NSTEMI treated with a drug-eluting stent to the proximal LAD. She felt steadily better with only mild afternoon fatigue and denied chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, lightheadedness, leg swelling, and bleeding. Home BP averaged 138/84 with HR 62, the inpatient echo showed LVEF 50%, and admission LDL was 118 mg/dL. The impression was clinically stable post-NSTEMI without angina, with hypertension above goal. Lisinopril 5 mg daily was started with a BMP in 1 to 2 weeks, other medications were continued, and a lipid panel, cardiac rehab referral, and ECG follow-up in 6 weeks were arranged.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. A professional interpreter is here with us, so please speak in short sentences and pause so the interpreter can translate. I see you are a 65-year-old male here about chest discomfort when you walk. Tell me about it.
Patient: Yes. For about three months, when I climb stairs or walk fast uphill, I feel pressure in the middle of my chest. It goes away if I stop and rest for about three minutes.
Doctor: Does the pressure spread to your arm, neck, or jaw? Do you get shortness of breath with it?
Patient: No, it stays in the middle. I don't have shortness of breath.
Doctor: Do you ever have pain at rest, or wake up at night with pain? Any fainting?
Patient: No pain at rest, no pain at night, and no fainting.
Doctor: Do you have other health problems, and what medicines do you take?
Patient: I have high blood pressure. I take amlodipine 5 mg every morning, and nothing else.
Doctor: Thank you. Your blood pressure today is 136/82 and your heart rate is 72. Your heart sounds regular with no murmur, your lungs are clear, and there is no leg swelling. The ECG we did when you arrived shows a normal rhythm with no acute changes.
Patient: So what is wrong with my heart?
Doctor: What you describe is stable exertional angina, which means the heart muscle is not getting enough blood flow when you exert yourself, most likely from narrowed heart arteries. Here is the plan. I will increase your amlodipine to 10 mg once daily. I am also prescribing nitroglycerin 0.4 mg tablets to put under your tongue if the pressure comes, and you can take one every 5 minutes, up to three tablets. If the pain is not better after the first tablet, call emergency services. I am also ordering an exercise stress test and blood tests for cholesterol, and I want to see you back in four weeks. The interpreter will go over the written instructions with you in your language.
Patient: Yes, I understand. Thank you, doctor.
summary: A 65-year-old male with high blood pressure was seen in cardiology with a professional interpreter for three months of chest discomfort on exertion, relieved by about three minutes of rest. He denied shortness of breath, pain at rest, pain at night, and fainting. Examination was unremarkable and the ECG showed a normal rhythm with no acute changes. The impression was stable exertional angina. Amlodipine was increased to 10 mg once daily, nitroglycerin 0.4 mg tablets under the tongue were prescribed, and an exercise stress test and cholesterol blood tests were ordered with return in four weeks.

soap.subjective: 65-year-old male seen with a professional interpreter for about three months of chest pressure when climbing stairs or walking fast uphill, relieved by about three minutes of rest. Denies spread of the pressure, shortness of breath, pain at rest, pain at night, and fainting. History of high blood pressure, taking amlodipine 5 mg every morning and no other medicines.
soap.objective: BP 136/82, heart rate 72. Heart sounds regular with no murmur, lungs clear, no leg swelling. ECG shows a normal rhythm with no acute changes.
soap.assessment: Stable exertional angina, most likely from narrowed heart arteries. High blood pressure.
plan: Increase amlodipine to 10 mg once daily
Prescribe nitroglycerin 0.4 mg tablets under the tongue as needed, one every 5 minutes up to three tablets; call emergency services if pain is not better after the first tablet
Order exercise stress test and blood tests for cholesterol
Return in four weeks
Interpreter to review written instructions with the patient

note:
The patient is a 52-year-old female seen in orthopedic clinic for follow-up of low back pain that radiates down the left leg. The pain began about five weeks ago after she lifted a heavy box and now runs from the left buttock to the outer calf and the top of the left foot. It is 7 out of 10 when sitting or coughing and eases when she stands or walks. She has numbness over the top of the left foot and has noticed her left big toe catching when she walks. She denies bowel or bladder dysfunction, saddle numbness, fever, weight loss, and any fall or other injury. She has hypertension and GERD. Her medications are lisinopril 10 mg daily and omeprazole 20 mg daily, plus over-the-counter naproxen 500 mg BID that has helped only partly and has caused epigastric burning for the past week.

On examination, BP 132/80 and HR 74. She walks with a mild antalgic gait. There is tenderness over the left L4-L5 paraspinal muscles. Straight leg raise is positive on the left at 40 degrees and negative on the right. Left great toe extension strength is 4/5, other muscle groups are 5/5, and sensation is decreased over the dorsum of the left foot. Patellar and Achilles reflexes are 2+ and symmetric.

I reviewed the MRI of the lumbar spine obtained two weeks ago, which shows an L4-L5 left paracentral disc protrusion contacting the traversing left L5 nerve root, with mild foraminal narrowing and no compression of the cauda equina.

My impression is left L5 radiculopathy from an L4-L5 disc herniation with a mild motor deficit. Her hypertension is controlled, and her GERD symptoms are aggravated by the naproxen. I advised her to stop naproxen and started prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days, and we discussed checking her home blood pressure during the course. I also started gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime. She will continue lisinopril and omeprazole. I referred her to physical therapy and encouraged her to stay active rather than rest in bed. If there is no improvement in 4 to 6 weeks, we will discuss an epidural steroid injection, and she was told to go to the emergency department immediately for new leg weakness, numbness in the groin, or loss of bladder or bowel control. Follow-up in 4 weeks.
summary: A 52-year-old female with hypertension and GERD presented to orthopedic clinic with five weeks of low back pain radiating down the left leg with numbness over the foot, without bowel or bladder dysfunction or saddle numbness. Examination showed a positive left straight leg raise, 4/5 left great toe extension, and decreased sensation over the dorsum of the left foot. MRI of the lumbar spine showed an L4-L5 left paracentral disc protrusion contacting the left L5 nerve root. Assessment was left L5 radiculopathy from an L4-L5 disc herniation with a mild motor deficit. Naproxen was stopped, prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days and gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime were started, and physical therapy and 4-week follow-up were arranged.

note:
Gynecology inpatient progress note, hospital day 2.

The patient is a 25-year-old female admitted yesterday with heavy vaginal bleeding. Her mother is at the bedside and reports that the patient soaked through a pad every hour for about six hours before arrival and that the heavy bleeding has lasted nine days. The patient confirms this and says her periods have been irregular for about a year. She denies fainting, fever, pelvic pain, and any recent injury. She has no chronic medical conditions and no known drug allergies.

Overnight the bleeding slowed to light spotting after starting norethindrone acetate 5 mg three times daily. This morning her blood pressure is 104/62 and heart rate is 96, and she is afebrile. She looks pale with pale conjunctivae. The abdomen is soft and nontender. On speculum exam there is a small amount of dark blood in the vagina with no active bleeding from the cervical os.

Hemoglobin was 8.9 on admission and 8.7 this morning. The urine pregnancy test is negative and the thyroid-stimulating hormone was normal. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal-sized uterus, an endometrial thickness of 9 mm, no fibroids or polyps, and normal ovaries.

My impression is abnormal uterine bleeding, most likely from ovulatory dysfunction, with acute blood loss anemia. I will continue norethindrone acetate 5 mg three times daily and start ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily. Hemoglobin will be repeated tomorrow morning. If the bleeding stays light she can go home tomorrow, and she will follow up in the gynecology clinic in two weeks to discuss long-term hormonal treatment.

She denied fainting, fever, pelvic pain, and recent injury. On hospital day 2 the bleeding had slowed to light spotting on norethindrone acetate, with BP 104/62, HR 96, hemoglobin 8.7, a negative pregnancy test, and a normal pelvic ultrasound. The impression was abnormal uterine bleeding, likely from ovulatory dysfunction, with acute blood loss anemia. Norethindrone acetate 5 mg three times daily was continued, ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily started, hemoglobin to be repeated, and gynecology follow-up arranged in two weeks.

Dictating a neurology clinic follow-up note. The patient is a 41-year-old male with type 2 diabetes for eight years who comes in for burning pain in both feet that has been getting worse over four months. The pain is worse at night and he rates it 6 out of 10. He also has some numbness in the toes. He denies weakness, foot ulcers, falls, and any change in bowel or bladder function. His only medication is metformin 1000 mg twice daily.

On exam blood pressure is 128/78 and heart rate 72. Strength is 5/5 throughout. Monofilament sensation is decreased over both great toes and the forefeet, and vibration sense is reduced at the toes. Ankle reflexes are diminished bilaterally, knee reflexes are normal, and gait is normal. There is no skin breakdown on the feet. Labs from last week show A1c 8.4 percent, correction, 8.1 percent, and a normal B12 level.

Impression is painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, length dependent, with suboptimal glucose control. Plan is to start pregabalin 75 mg twice daily and I counseled him about drowsiness and dizziness. He will continue metformin, work on diet and exercise with a goal A1c below 7 percent, do daily foot checks, and return to clinic in four weeks. That completes the dictation.

note:
This is a dictation for a gastroenterology inpatient progress note on hospital day 3. The patient is a 53-year-old female with ulcerative colitis admitted with a flare, and I am dictating after seeing her on the ward and speaking with the pharmacist and the social worker.

Interval history. She was admitted three days ago with about ten bloody stools a day, correction, eight bloody stools a day, along with abdominal cramping, urgency, and nocturnal stools for two weeks. Overnight she had four bloody stools, down from six the night before, and she says the cramping is better. She had mild fatigue and a low-grade fever on admission, and the fever has resolved. She denies vomiting, severe abdominal pain, and shortness of breath.

Medication history and cost. On admission she told the team she had stopped her mesalamine altogether six weeks ago because the copay went up after her insurance changed. On further questioning today she clarified, correction, that she did not stop it. She has been taking 2.4 g once daily, half of the prescribed 4.8 g once daily, by cutting her tablets to stretch the supply. She has also been taking over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg as needed for joint pain several times a week. Her other history includes hypertension, hypothyroidism, gastroesophageal reflux, and osteopenia. Her other home medications are levothyroxine 88 mcg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. She has no known drug allergies.

Inpatient medications so far are IV methylprednisolone 40 mg every 12 hours since admission, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for prophylaxis, and one dose of potassium chloride 40 mEq by mouth yesterday for low potassium.

Vitals this morning are temperature 98.6, blood pressure 128/76, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. She looks tired but not toxic. The abdomen is soft with mild left lower quadrant tenderness, no distension, no rebound, and no guarding, and bowel sounds are present. There is no peripheral edema, no oral ulcers, and no joint effusions.

Data. Hemoglobin 10.2, white count 11.8, platelets 410, albumin 2.9, CRP 48 mg/L, potassium 3.4 on admission and 3.9 after repletion, and creatinine 0.8. Stool C. difficile PCR and stool cultures are negative. Abdominal x-ray shows no colonic dilation and no free air. Flexible sigmoidoscopy has not been done yet.

Assessment and plan. She has a moderate to severe ulcerative colitis flare, precipitated by under-dosing of mesalamine because of cost and by NSAID use, and it is responding to IV steroids. She also has anemia and hypokalemia, which is improving, and her hypertension and hypothyroidism are stable. Today I am switching IV methylprednisolone to oral prednisone 40 mg daily. I am increasing mesalamine back to the full 4.8 g once daily. I am stopping ibuprofen and she is to avoid all NSAIDs, using acetaminophen for joint pain instead. Continue levothyroxine, lisinopril, omeprazole, and enoxaparin. Repeat CBC and basic metabolic panel in the morning. Flexible sigmoidoscopy tomorrow to assess severity before deciding on a biologic, with hepatitis B serologies and QuantiFERON sent today in case a biologic is needed. The social worker and pharmacist will help her apply for a manufacturer assistance program and will find a lower cost mesalamine formulation. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation given steroid exposure and osteopenia. If she continues to improve she may go home in two days, with gastroenterology clinic follow-up in two weeks. That completes the dictation.

She first said she had stopped mesalamine but clarified she was taking half the prescribed dose because of cost, and she also used ibuprofen. Hemoglobin was 10.2 and CRP 48 mg/L, infectious stool studies were negative, and abdominal x-ray showed no colonic dilation. IV methylprednisolone was changed to prednisone 40 mg daily, mesalamine was increased to 4.8 g once daily, and ibuprofen was stopped. Flexible sigmoidoscopy, pre-biologic screening, cost-assistance referrals, and clinic follow-up in two weeks were planned.

The patient is a 50-year-old male seen in urology clinic for an elevated PSA of 5.8 ng/mL found on a routine physical, up from 2.1 ng/mL two years ago. He was visibly anxious and asked many questions throughout the visit, including whether this means he has cancer, whether he needs a biopsy today, and whether his father's history changes his risk. His father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at age 62. I answered each question, and he asked for written information, which I provided.

He reports waking to urinate twice a night and a weaker urinary stream for about a year. He denies hematuria, dysuria, fever, bone pain, and unintentional weight loss. He has hypertension treated with lisinopril 20 mg daily. He has also been taking over-the-counter saw palmetto 320 mg daily for urinary symptoms.

On examination, BP 136/84 and HR 80. The abdomen is soft without suprapubic tenderness. Digital rectal exam shows a mildly enlarged, smooth, symmetric, non-tender prostate with no nodules. Urinalysis is negative for blood, leukocytes, and nitrites. Free PSA is 14%.

I explained in plain terms that a PSA can be raised by benign prostate enlargement, inflammation, recent ejaculation, or cycling, and that most men with this level do not have cancer, but that further evaluation is appropriate. We discussed the MRI-first approach, what a biopsy involves, and the likely timeline, and he said he felt calmer afterward.

My impression is elevated PSA with lower urinary tract symptoms, most likely related to benign prostatic hyperplasia, with a family history in his father that raises concern. I recommend a repeat PSA in 6 weeks after avoiding ejaculation and cycling for 48 hours beforehand, and a multiparametric prostate MRI. I started tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily for his urinary symptoms and asked him to stop saw palmetto. He will continue lisinopril. A biopsy will be considered if the MRI is suspicious or the PSA stays elevated. He will return in 2 weeks to review results, and I gave him the clinic nurse line for questions in the meantime.

The plan was a repeat PSA in 6 weeks, a multiparametric prostate MRI, tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, and stopping saw palmetto, with return in 2 weeks.

note:
The patient is a 28-year-old male seen in the family medicine clinic for sneezing, a runny nose, and itchy eyes that return every spring and have been much worse for the last three weeks. He works outdoors on a landscaping crew. He has limited health literacy, so I used plain language, short sentences, and the teach-back method throughout the visit and used his pill bottles to check his medicines.

He describes clear runny nose, fits of sneezing, itchy watery eyes, and an itchy throat, with a mild cough at night. Symptoms are worse when he is mowing or working in tall grass and better on rainy days. He has had the same pattern every spring since his teens. He denies fever, facial pain, wheezing, and chest tightness. Since his last visit he denies leg swelling, calf pain, bleeding, and black stools.

His history includes a DVT in the left leg two years ago, asthma, GERD, and anxiety. When I asked about his blood thinner, he first said he takes apixaban "one pill a day." His bottle reads 5 mg twice a day. After we counted the pills left in the bottle and went over his morning and evening routine, he confirmed that he takes one pill in the morning and one at night, so the correct dose is apixaban 5 mg twice daily. Other prescribed medications are an albuterol inhaler 2 puffs as needed, used about twice a week, omeprazole 20 mg daily, sertraline 50 mg daily, and fluticasone nasal spray, 1 spray in each nostril once daily, which he uses only on bad days and aims straight up the middle of his nose. Over the counter he takes pseudoephedrine 60 mg every 6 hours for stuffiness, diphenhydramine 25 mg at night, and ibuprofen 400 mg twice a week for sinus headaches. I told him that ibuprofen can cause bleeding when taken with apixaban.

On examination, BP 142/90, HR 82, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 98.4 F. He is comfortable. The nasal turbinates are pale and boggy with clear drainage, there are no polyps, and there is no sinus tenderness. He has allergic shiners and watery red conjunctivae. The throat shows cobblestoning without exudate. Lungs are clear with no wheezes. There is no leg swelling or calf tenderness, and no bruising.

Recent results: CBC last month showed hemoglobin 14.8 and platelets 245. Creatinine was 0.9. An allergen-specific IgE panel was positive for grass and ragweed pollen.

My impression is seasonal allergic rhinitis with allergic conjunctivitis. It is poorly controlled because of his nasal spray technique and his use of over-the-counter pseudoephedrine, diphenhydramine, and ibuprofen. His blood pressure is mildly elevated, probably from the pseudoephedrine. His asthma is well controlled, and his GERD and anxiety are stable. He remains on apixaban for the prior DVT.

I increased fluticasone to 2 sprays in each nostril once daily and showed him how to aim the spray toward the outer wall of each nostril, away from the middle; he demonstrated it back correctly. I started loratadine 10 mg once daily. I told him to stop pseudoephedrine, stop diphenhydramine, and stop ibuprofen. For headaches he can use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed. He must keep taking apixaban 5 mg twice daily and should never skip it, and we made a picture-based medicine chart with a pillbox for morning and night. He will continue albuterol, omeprazole, and sertraline. A nurse will recheck his blood pressure in 2 weeks. He should call or come in for bleeding, black stools, calf swelling, wheezing, or trouble breathing. I gave him a one-page handout with pictures, and he will return in 4 weeks.
summary: A 28-year-old male with limited health literacy and a prior DVT on apixaban presented to family medicine with spring sneezing, runny nose, and itchy eyes, much worse for three weeks. He denied fever, facial pain, wheezing, chest tightness, and bleeding. He first said he took apixaban once a day, but the bottle and pill count confirmed 5 mg twice daily. The impression was seasonal allergic rhinitis with allergic conjunctivitis, poorly controlled because of spray technique and over-the-counter pseudoephedrine, diphenhydramine, and ibuprofen, with BP 142/90. Fluticasone was increased to 2 sprays per nostril daily, loratadine started, those three over-the-counter drugs stopped with acetaminophen for headaches, and a BP recheck in 2 weeks and follow-up in 4 weeks arranged.

note:
The patient is a 44-year-old female seen in neurology clinic three weeks after an emergency department visit for a transient ischemic attack. At that time she had sudden right arm weakness and slurred speech lasting about 20 minutes that had resolved completely before she arrived. She has had no further episodes. She denies headache, vision loss, double vision, and palpitations, and has had no new numbness. She has hyperlipidemia and no other chronic conditions. She was started on aspirin 81 mg daily and clopidogrel 75 mg daily in the emergency department for 21 days, and on atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. She also uses over-the-counter supplements, ginkgo biloba 120 mg daily for memory and fish oil 1000 mg daily, and she thought they would protect her brain.

On examination, BP 126/78 and HR 72. She is alert with fluent speech, no facial droop, no pronator drift, strength 5/5 in all limbs, intact sensation, and a normal gait. There is no carotid bruit.

I reviewed her results. MRI of the brain with diffusion imaging showed no acute infarct. MRA of the head and neck showed no stenosis. Echocardiogram with a bubble study showed normal ejection fraction and no PFO. LDL was 142 mg/dL when checked at the time of the event, and A1c was 5.6%. A 30-day cardiac event monitor is in progress.

My impression is a transient ischemic attack of uncertain mechanism, most likely small vessel or atherosclerotic given her LDL, with no evidence of atrial fibrillation so far. Her hyperlipidemia is not at goal. Today is day 21 of dual antiplatelet therapy, so I stopped clopidogrel and she will continue aspirin 81 mg daily long term. I increased atorvastatin from 40 mg to 80 mg nightly, with a goal LDL below 70. I told her to stop ginkgo biloba because it can increase bleeding risk with antiplatelet medicines, and she may continue fish oil. She should bring all her supplement bottles to future visits. I will wait for the final event monitor result and order a fasting lipid panel in 6 to 8 weeks. I reviewed stroke warning signs and calling 911 immediately for any new weakness, speech change, or vision loss. Follow-up in clinic in 3 months.
summary: A 44-year-old female with hyperlipidemia was seen in neurology three weeks after a transient ischemic attack with 20 minutes of right arm weakness and slurred speech and no recurrence. She was also using over-the-counter ginkgo biloba and fish oil. Neurologic exam was normal, MRI of the brain and MRA of the head and neck showed no acute infarct or stenosis, echocardiogram showed no PFO, and LDL was 142 mg/dL. Clopidogrel was stopped after 21 days with aspirin continued, atorvastatin was increased to 80 mg nightly, and ginkgo biloba was stopped for bleeding risk. A fasting lipid panel in 6 to 8 weeks, the 30-day event monitor result, and follow-up in 3 months were planned.

LDL 142 mg/dL at the time of the event, A1c 5.6%. 30-day cardiac event monitor in progress.
soap.assessment: Transient ischemic attack of uncertain mechanism, most likely small vessel or atherosclerotic given LDL, with no evidence of atrial fibrillation so far. Hyperlipidemia not at goal.
plan: Stop clopidogrel (day 21 of dual antiplatelet therapy); continue aspirin 81 mg daily long term
Increase atorvastatin from 40 mg to 80 mg nightly, goal LDL below 70
Stop ginkgo biloba because of bleeding risk with antiplatelet medicines; may continue fish oil; bring all supplement bottles to future visits
Await final 30-day cardiac event monitor result
Fasting lipid panel in 6 to 8 weeks
Reviewed stroke warning signs; call 911 immediately for new weakness, speech change, or vision loss
Follow up in clinic in 3 months

summary: A 62-year-old female with hypertension, osteopenia, and primary hyperparathyroidism that was never followed up, who has limited health literacy, was seen in the emergency department for 2 weeks of nausea, constipation, polyuria, and increased thirst with feeling foggy. She denied vomiting, abdominal pain, chest pain, palpitations, fever, and head trauma. Calcium was 13.2 with PTH 148 and creatinine 1.3 from a baseline of 0.9, and the ECG showed a short QTc. The impression was symptomatic hypercalcemia from primary hyperparathyroidism worsened by HCTZ, calcium, and dehydration, with mild prerenal AKI. She received normal saline and zoledronic acid, HCTZ and calcium were stopped, amlodipine was started, and she was admitted with endocrine surgery referral planned.
